questions.question_text:
A ball is projected at $50^{\circ}$ above the horizontal.
Use the simple projectile model with $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$ and up as positive.
What are its horizontal and vertical accelerations?

options.why: Makes gravity act upwards; in the simple model, gravity is the only force and acts downwards.
Places gravitational acceleration horizontally; the simple model assumes gravity acts vertically only.
Ignores gravitational acceleration; neglecting air resistance in the simple model still leaves gravity acting.

questions.solution_text:
In the simple model, air resistance is ignored and gravity is the only force acting.
$\ddot{x}=0$
$\ddot{y}=-10$

questions.question_text: In the simple projectile model, what is the only force acting on the object during its flight?

options.why: Names the force that the simple model ignores, rather than the force it retains.

options.text: The force from the thrower's hand
options.why: Treats the launch force as continuing after the object has left the hand.
Confuses ignoring air resistance with ignoring gravity as well.

questions.solution_text: Gravity is the only force acting in the simple projectile model, which ignores air resistance.

questions.question_text:
A ball is projected at $35^{\circ}$ above the horizontal with speed $22\text{ m/s}$.
Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with up as positive.
What are $\ddot{x}$ and $\ddot{y}$? Give numerical accelerations in $\text{m/s}^{2}$ to 2 d.p. where necessary.

options.why: Used $-10\sin35^{\circ}$ for the vertical acceleration, resolving gravity along the launch direction instead of using the whole downward value.
Used $-10\cos35^{\circ}$ and $-10\sin35^{\circ}$, resolving gravity into both components, but gravity acts vertically only.
Used $-10\cos35^{\circ}$ horizontally, applying gravity to the horizontal component as well, but there is no horizontal force.

questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown into the air and reaches the highest point of its flight.
Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with $\underset{\sim}{j}$ pointing **downwards** as the positive vertical direction.
Which vector is the acceleration of the ball at that instant?

options.why: Wrote the usual $-g\underset{\sim}{j}$ from memory without noticing that this stem takes downwards as positive.
Put the gravity term in the horizontal component instead of the vertical one.
Both slips at once: gravity placed horizontally and copied with the sign of the up-positive convention.

questions.solution_text:
The acceleration of a projectile is constant, and gravity acts downwards at every instant, including the highest point.
Downwards is positive here, so the vertical component is $+10$.
$\underset{\sim}{\ddot{r}}=0\underset{\sim}{i}+10\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=10\underset{\sim}{j}$

questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown with speed $40\text{ m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal.
Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)$ in exact form?

options.why: Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Made the vertical component negative, although the ball is thrown upwards.
Both slips: the ratios swapped and the upward component taken as negative.

questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown from the top of a wall $5\text{ m}$ above the ground with speed $14\text{ m/s}$ at $20^{\circ}$ above the horizontal.
Which is its initial velocity vector? Give components in $\text{m/s}$ to 2 d.p.

options.why: Makes the vertical component negative, although the ball is thrown above the horizontal.
Swaps sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Swaps sine and cosine and makes the upward vertical component negative.

questions.question_text:
A stone is thrown from a cliff at $28^{\circ}$ **below** the horizontal with speed $15\text{ m/s}$.
Which pair gives its initial horizontal and vertical velocity components? Give components in $\text{m/s}$ to 2 d.p.

options.why: Makes the vertical component positive, although the stone is thrown below the horizontal.
Uses sine for the horizontal component and cosine for the vertical component.
Swaps sine and cosine and makes the downward vertical component positive.

questions.question_text:
A projectile is launched from the origin with initial velocity $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=-9\underset{\sim}{i}+12\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second.
What is its launch speed and direction, with the angle to 1 d.p.?

options.text: $15\text{ m/s}$, at $53.1^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
$15\text{ m/s}$, at $36.9^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
options.why: Used $\tan\alpha=\frac{9}{12}$, inverting the ratio of vertical to horizontal component.

options.text: $21\text{ m/s}$, at $53.1^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
options.why: Added the two component sizes instead of using Pythagoras to find the speed.

options.text: $21\text{ m/s}$, at $36.9^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
options.why: Both slips: components added for the speed and the tangent ratio inverted.

questions.solution_text:
$V=\sqrt{(-9)^{2}+12^{2}}$
$=\sqrt{225}$
$=15$
$\tan\alpha=\dfrac{12}{9}$
$\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$
$\approx 53.1^{\circ}$
The launch speed is $15\text{ m/s}$ at $53.1^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, directed to the left.

questions.question_text: Take $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^{2}$. If $\mathbf j$ points directly upwards, which of these describes the acceleration of a projectile?

options.why: Points upward, but gravitational acceleration acts downward.
Adds an unjustified horizontal component and makes the vertical component positive, although gravity acts downwards.
Ignores the constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

questions.solution_text: With upward represented by positive $\mathbf j$, gravity acts in the negative vertical direction. The acceleration vector is therefore $0\mathbf i-9.8\mathbf j=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-9.8\end{pmatrix}$.
